strengths: The paper targets a well-motivated practical problem (single-step, low-latency generative policies for robot manipulation) and builds incrementally but sensibly on a recent and relevant baseline (MP1/MeanFlow).
The proposed Cosine/Directional Alignment loss is simple, lightweight, and easy to integrate into existing MeanFlow-based training pipelines without adding network depth or parameters.

Empirical results on a fairly large task suite (37 tasks across Adroit and Meta-World, 3 seeds) show consistent and, on harder task subsets (Medium/Hard/Very-Hard Meta-World), sizeable improvements over MP1 and FlowPolicy while retaining single-step (NFE=1) inference speed.
The ablation study (Table 2) isolates the contribution of the dispersive loss, the cosine loss, and the DDE approximation, giving some insight into which component drives the improvement.
The paper is reasonably well organized with a clear related-work positioning relative to diffusion-based, flow-based, and MeanFlow-based policies.
weaknesses: The abstract explicitly claims OMP addresses MP1's 'lack of few-shot generalization,' but no experiment varies the number of demonstrations or otherwise directly measures few-shot generalization; the only evidence offered is standard success-rate comparisons under a fixed 10-demo setting, so this central claim is unsupported by the experiments provided.

The theoretical motivation (Section 4.2) treats generic high-dimensional MSE regression gradient starvation as a novel finding, but the argument is elementary vector calculus (Law of Cosines) and does not rigorously connect to the specific structure of the MeanFlow identity (Eq. 4) that the model actually optimizes; the paper aligns predictions with v0 = zT − z0 (the full 0-to-1 displacement) even though training samples arbitrary sub-intervals [r,t], and the assumption that the local average velocity over [r,t] should point in the same direction as the global displacement is not justified or discussed, especially for curved/multimodal trajectories.

The claimed reduction in GPU memory usage from replacing JVP with the Differential Derivation Equation (DDE) is never quantified (no memory numbers, no wall-clock comparison); only a success-rate ablation is reported, which actually shows a performance drop, making the practical value of this contribution unclear.

Equation (11), which defines the DDE approximation, contains an apparent typo/inconsistency in the argument ordering of the two terms in the numerator, undermining confidence in the correctness of the reported method.

Key hyperparameters (λ_Disp, λ_cos, the perturbation constant ϵ in DDE, and cosine-loss temperature) are never specified with concrete values, and no code release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility.

Improvements over MP1 are modest and, for several task categories, fall within or close to overlapping standard deviations (e.g., Hard tasks: 62.5±3.1 vs. 58.1±5.0), raising questions about statistical significance given only 3 random seeds.

DM1, described in the related work as the most closely related concurrent method (also using MeanFlow + dispersive regularization for one-step manipulation), is not included in the main quantitative comparison table, leaving an important direct baseline comparison missing.
The manuscript contains multiple typographical and formatting issues (e.g., 'twnety-one', inconsistent notation in Eq. 11, unclear task splits/counts) that detract from polish and clarity.

strengths: The paper identifies and motivates a concrete, underexplored problem when applying the MeanFlow paradigm to robotic manipulation: spectral bias (low-pass filtering behavior of the averaging operator), gradient starvation in low-velocity/high-precision regimes, and the memory overhead of nested JVP computations. These are illustrated with both toy synthetic experiments (Fig. 2) and closed-form derivations (Appendix B).

The proposed fix (directional alignment via cosine-similarity loss decoupled from magnitude, plus a finite-difference Differential Derivation Equation approximating the JVP) is simple, lightweight, and directly targets the diagnosed failure modes, making the contribution interpretable and easy to implement.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 37 simulated tasks (Adroit + Meta-World, stratified by difficulty) and 3 real-world manipulation tasks, with multiple seeds, ablations isolating the dispersive loss and directional alignment terms, and a sensitivity study over action-chunk horizons (Appendix E) and a JVP-vs-DDE memory/accuracy trade-off analysis (Table 3).

OMP shows consistent, and on harder task subsets (Meta-World Medium/Hard/Very Hard, real-world Slip Ring) substantial, improvements over strong recent baselines (MP1, FlowPolicy, DP3) while retaining single-step (NFE=1) inference, and exhibits qualitatively more stable training curves (Fig. 5) than baselines.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis, while presented with formal notation (Theorem B.1, gradient decompositions), rests on simplified linear/toy assumptions (e.g., treating trajectories as stationary stochastic processes, continuous-time gradient flow rather than the Adam optimizer actually used) and is validated only on small synthetic examples (sum-of-sines, 2D toy vectors); it is not clearly established that these idealized derivations transfer to the nonlinear, high-dimensional point-cloud policy networks used in the main experiments.

The core methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: a cosine-similarity alignment loss is a well-known technique, the dispersive loss is adopted from prior work (Geng et al., 2025a), and the finite-difference derivative approximation is explicitly motivated by Wang et al. (2025c). The main new element is the specific combination for MeanFlow policies, a modest algorithmic contribution relative to the strong theoretical framing in the paper.

Improvements over the strongest baseline (MP1) are fairly small in aggregate (82.3% vs 78.9%, a 3.4-point gain) and most of the gain is concentrated in a subset of harder tasks; on easy tasks performance is near-saturated, and the ablation shows directional alignment alone contributes only ~4 points, tempering claims that this mechanism is a 'critical' fix.

The DDE approximation introduces a free hyperparameter (perturbation constant epsilon) whose selection, stability, and sensitivity are not analyzed, despite this component being central to the claimed memory-efficiency contribution.

Real-world evaluation is based on only 20 trials per task across 3 tasks with no reported variance/confidence intervals, and neither simulated nor real-world results include formal statistical significance testing across seeds/trials, weakening confidence in the reported margins.

The abstract/claims mention improvements in 'trajectory accuracy,' but no explicit trajectory-accuracy metric (e.g., trajectory MSE, DTW) is reported in the main results — only success rate — creating a mismatch between stated contributions and presented evidence.

Presentation has some inconsistencies (e.g., unclear which OMP variant, JVP or DDE, corresponds to 'Ours' in Figure 1; minor grammatical issues) and reproducibility relies on supplementary material/code that is not independently verifiable in the review process.
